title: Quantum-safe security starts with ordinary computers
summary: Why preparing for quantum computers means changing the mathematics behind digital security.
author: Quantum Research Center

sections.heading: The change already has a starting point
paragraphs: On 13 August 2024, NIST announced approval of three post-quantum cryptography standards. One provides a way for communicating parties to establish a shared secret; two concern digital signatures, which help verify who signed data and whether it has changed.

sections.heading: What does “post-quantum” mean?
paragraphs: These methods run on conventional computers. Their mathematics is designed to withstand attacks from both conventional and future quantum computers. That is different from sending quantum states through a special communication link.

sections.heading: Why prepare ahead of time?
paragraphs: A sufficiently capable quantum computer could undermine widely used public-key cryptography. Information intercepted today may still be sensitive when a future attacker can decrypt it, and replacing cryptography across existing systems takes time.

sections.heading: What the milestone does—and does not—show
paragraphs: A published standard gives implementers a common specification. It does not mean every service has adopted it, or that an encryption-breaking quantum computer has been built. When reading a rollout announcement, look for which systems changed and what independent testing was performed.

sources.title: NIST: approval of three post-quantum standards (13 August 2024)
